elements.element: Customer has no duty to disclose to Vendor any third-party commercial offer for MFN purposes.
elements.evidence: Section 7.2 expressly states that Customer has no obligation to disclose any commercial offer it receives.

elements.element: Customer has no duty to match, equal, or extend to Vendor any more favourable third-party commercial terms.
elements.evidence: Section 7.2 expressly states that Customer has no obligation to match for Vendor any commercial offer it receives.

elements.element: Customer is subject to no other most-favoured-nation or most-favoured-customer commitment.
elements.evidence: Section 12.3 confirms that Customer has made no most-favoured-customer commitment, and Section 7.2 eliminates the specific MFN duties previously imposed.

elements.element: If an MFN obligation burdens Customer, it applies only to an expressly defined product.
elements.evidence: The condition is demonstrably absent: Sections 7.2 and 12.3 establish that no MFN obligation burdens Customer, so no broader product scope remains.

elements.element: If an MFN obligation burdens Customer, it lasts no more than 12 months.
elements.evidence: The condition is demonstrably absent: the rendered language imposes no MFN obligation on Customer, including one extending beyond 12 months.

elements.element: If an MFN obligation burdens Customer, it contains carve-outs excluding offers that are not reasonably comparable.
elements.evidence: The condition is demonstrably absent: because no MFN obligation applies, Customer cannot be required to compare or match non-comparable offers.

result.reason: The redline removes both operative duties—disclosure and matching—and retains the broader acknowledgement that Customer made no most-favoured-customer commitment. It therefore reaches the preferred position; the fallback limitations are also satisfied because their condition, an MFN burdening Customer, is expressly absent. The change is confined to the offending provision and does not restrict MFN pricing or protections running in Customer's favour. Drafting is effective, though “match for Vendor any commercial offer” is somewhat awkward and could more precisely refer to matching the terms of an offer.
